text:
Recent work supports exploring content-aware item representations, but the search found no verified 2024–2026 study matching all requirements: BERT4Rec, jointly trained ID plus title/description encoding, random initialization, and lightweight computation. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) combines titles, descriptions and reviews with self-attention; its reported gains depend substantially on reviews, unavailable here. [DenseRec (2025)](https://earl-workshop.github.io/pdf/recsys2025-workshops_paper_167.pdf) identifies a relevant limitation: semantic similarity can miss item-specific appeal. It learns content projections alongside ID representations, but uses pretrained embeddings and evaluates a SASRec extension, so it provides motivation rather than a directly compliant implementation.

A reasonable experimental hypothesis—not an established result from these papers—is a small, randomly initialized token embedding encoder with separate pooled title and description vectors, projected into the ID embedding dimension and combined through a jointly learned residual gate inside one BERT4Rec network. Retain ID embeddings to preserve item specificity; truncate text and encode only required unique items to control training cost. Masked positions must conceal both item IDs and their text features, with appended-mask inference. Compare against ID-only BERT4Rec using identical splits, seeds, training limits and macro validation HR@10, while measuring runtime. Shared words may help sparse items, but purpose, compatibility, ownership and entertainment preferences remain hypotheses unless supported by observed interactions; text similarity alone does not establish them.
